\subsection{Uncalibrated simulation}\label{sec:sim}

The propositions hold inside their model. This subsection asks two further
questions by discrete-event simulation. First, does a simulation that
satisfies a proposition's assumptions reproduce its closed form? Second,
when an assumption is dropped, does the decision the proposition implies
survive? The simulator is not calibrated. Its parameters are
illustrative, and every number below is a property of the simulated
model under a synthetic workload. None is a measurement of a serving
system, and none replaces an entry of \S\ref{sec:exp}. The calibrated
simulator of \S\ref{sec:exp-setup} will extend this one.

\paragraph{Simulator.} \texttt{libqueuingsim} is an event-driven
simulator written in Rust. It has five models: an open G/G/$c$ FIFO
queue, cross-checked against Lindley's recursion; closed or open agent
programs on one replica with a finite KV pool; offline eviction
instances with an exact dynamic-programming optimum; aggregated and
disaggregated PD pools (used in Appendix~\ref{app:pd}); and replicas with per-program KV locality. The
service time of a turn that appends $n$ tokens to a resident prefix of
$k$ tokens and decodes $o$ tokens is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sim-cost}
  S = s_0 + a\,n + b\,n\,(k + n/2) + d\,o .
\end{equation}
A miss re-prefills the whole context ($k=0$, $n$ equal to the context
length), so its cost is quadratic in context length, as in
ThunderAgent's Lemma~4.1 \citep{thunderagent}. We use $s_0=5$\,ms,
$a=2\cdot10^{-5}$\,s, $b=2\cdot10^{-9}$\,s and $d=2\cdot10^{-4}$\,s per
token. Whether a program issues another turn is drawn when its tool call
returns. A suspended program therefore holds KV that may never be
reused, which is what gives the resume probability $p_i$ a role in
eviction. The replica serves one turn at a time, so continuous batching
is not modelled.

\paragraph{Checks.} Each proposition is turned into a named check with
fixed seeds and an explicit tolerance. An \emph{in-model} check keeps the
proposition's assumptions, so a failure would indicate a bug in the
simulator or in the closed form. A \emph{beyond-model} check drops an
assumption: non-Poisson arrivals, a hit rate that emerges from finite
memory, tandem pools with integer splits, or a heuristic controller in
place of the optimum. Of \simChecks{} checks, \simChecksPassed{} pass.
Confidence intervals are 95\,\% batch means (20 batches) or, where
stated, across independent seeds. Every table in this subsection is
generated by the simulator from fixed seeds.

\input{sim/tab-inmodel}

\subsubsection{In-model: the closed forms}\label{sec:sim-inmodel}

Table~\ref{tab:sim-inmodel} compares closed forms with simulation under
their own assumptions. Workload A has deterministic unit service;
workload B has the same mean with service $0.1$ w.p.\ $3/4$ and $3.7$
w.p.\ $1/4$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:pk} predicts a wait ratio of
$3.43$ at every load. The cache row uses $S^{\mathrm{hit}}=0.05$,
$S^{\mathrm{miss}}=0.5$ and $\lambda=1.8$, where $\rho$ falls from $0.9$
at $p=0$ to $0.252$ at $p=0.8$. The M/M/1 response time, the PK wait,
the variance ratio, the utilisation and the $(1+\mathrm{CV}^2)/2$ ratio
of Eq.~\eqref{eq:cv2} agree to within the confidence interval or
2\,\%.
Over 9000 random eviction instances with equal $p_i$, the worst
shortest-first cost is below twice the optimum, as
Proposition~\ref{prop:evict}(ii) requires. These checks confirm the
simulator, not the propositions, which are already proved.

\subsubsection{Beyond the model}\label{sec:sim-beyond}

\input{sim/tab-kingman}

\paragraph{Bursty arrivals.} Table~\ref{tab:sim-kingman} keeps the
agentic service law of Eq.~\eqref{eq:cv2} and replaces Poisson arrivals
with hyperexponential ones. The PK formula underestimates the simulated
wait, and the gap grows with the interarrival variability. Kingman's
bound holds in every row. This is the direction stated in
\S\ref{sec:limits}: arrival variability adds to service variability.

\input{sim/tab-closed}

\paragraph{Emergent hit rate.} In Table~\ref{tab:sim-closed} the hit rate
is not an input. It results from memory pressure among $N$ closed
programs whose KV stays resident during tool calls. As $N$ grows, the
hit rate falls, $\E[S]$ rises and throughput falls. This is the mechanism
of \S\ref{sec:model}: in a closed network with fixed per-visit demand,
throughput does not decrease with $N$, so a falling throughput signals a
growing demand per step. With ample memory every follow-up turn hits,
and the simulated throughput is non-decreasing in $N$ and stays below the
asymptotic bound $\min(N/(D+Z),1/D)$ \citep{lazowska1984}, where $D$ is the
mean service demand and $Z$ the mean think time. The collapse in
Table~\ref{tab:sim-closed} therefore comes from the finite pool. The
interactive response-time law holds to
within 0.3\,\%. The simulation shows that the mechanism is sufficient to
produce a throughput collapse. It does not show that this mechanism
caused the collapse reported by ThunderAgent.

\input{sim/tab-offload}

\paragraph{Offloading.} Table~\ref{tab:sim-offload} compares three
offloading policies on the closed workload. With blocking fetches the
replica waits for the tier. Always-offload then falls below
never-offload when the tier is slow (5k and 20k tokens/s), which is the
second observation of \S\ref{sec:offload}. The selective policy
chooses per program between fetching and recomputing. It compares the
tier wait plus transfer time with the recompute time $\Delta S_i$. It is
within 3\,\% of the better fixed policy, or above it, in
\simOffloadOk{} of \simOffloadCells{} cells. The option-value argument of \S\ref{sec:offload}
concerns the optimal controller. This rule is a heuristic, so the result
is evidence that a simple rule captures most of the option value in this
model, not a consequence of that argument. The last column shows that
the collapse depends on the fetch being on the critical path. With
asynchronous fetches, always-offload has the highest throughput at every
bandwidth, even when the tier is saturated. Programs waiting for the
tier hold no device memory, so the tier queue acts as admission control
and the remaining programs hit. Whether real stacks fetch synchronously
is a property of the implementation that E3 must record.

\input{sim/tab-evict}
\input{sim/tab-evict-dyn}

\paragraph{Eviction.} Offline (Table~\ref{tab:sim-evict}), the
simulation reproduces the three regimes of
Proposition~\ref{prop:evict}. With equal $p_i$, shortest-first and the
density rule choose the same programs and stay within a factor of~2 of
the optimum. When $p_i$ varies, shortest-first reaches ten times the
optimum on some instances, and the density rule of
Theorem~\ref{thm:dantzig} stays much closer on average. The dynamic
result differs (Table~\ref{tab:sim-evict-dyn}). Inside the closed system,
eviction decisions repeat and freed memory is reused. Here the density rule orders by the
expected recompute cost per token, $p_i\,\Delta S_i/c_i$ with $\Delta
S_i$ from Eq.~\eqref{eq:sim-cost}. Across five seeds its throughput is
not distinguishable from shortest-first's, while LRU is lower at every
$N$. In this scenario the offline gap between the two rules does not
carry over to throughput. Problem~\eqref{eq:evict} is a one-step
approximation of~\eqref{eq:mdp}, and the simulation suggests that E4
should report end-to-end metrics next to cost/OPT. This is one synthetic
two-class mix; we do not claim that the result holds for real traces.

\input{sim/tab-routing}

\paragraph{Routing.} Table~\ref{tab:sim-routing} routes follow-up turns
over four replicas when half of the new programs start on replica~0.
Under strict affinity that skew is permanent. Once replica~0 saturates,
the affinity response time rises by two orders of magnitude, while the
lookahead rule~\eqref{eq:lookahead} stays flat. This is
the behaviour of Proposition~\ref{prop:routing} in a network with
correlated arrivals. The lookahead rule may migrate KV or recompute on
another replica, whichever is cheaper. Migration is cheap in this
scenario ($2\cdot10^6$ tokens/s). With costlier migration the load at
which affinity loses would move, and E6 measures it. The KV-aware myopic
rule, which may only recompute away from the KV, lies between the two.

\subsubsection{What the simulation does not show}\label{sec:sim-limits}

The simulator shares the model's abstractions. It does not model
continuous batching, block-level KV allocation, partial prefix hits,
collective-communication contention, and it
serves one turn at a time per replica. Its parameters were chosen to be
plausible, not measured. Its results therefore show which decisions are
robust to the assumptions we dropped. They say nothing about how often
each regime occurs in practice. The experiments of \S\ref{sec:exp},
starting with the calibration of E1, remain necessary.
